JusPrin compiles from source on the Windows test VM and the built binary runs
with its Agent UI visible. Verified 2026-09-07 on n2-standard-16: deps 22.7 min,
slicer 23.0 min. Output is `orca-slicer.exe` (261 KB launcher) plus

`/Users/kenneth/jusprin-win-vm-harness/BUILDING.md`; VM setup in its README.
See [[windows-gui-test-vm-gcp]].

**Why:** four of the five failures below produce misleading errors far from
their cause, and two were self-inflicted by how the build was driven.

**How to apply:**
- Run long builds as a Windows **scheduled task** (SYSTEM / ServiceAccount), not
  over SSH — OpenSSH kills the process tree on disconnect. Never let two builds
  share a directory: that produced OpenSSL `C1033 cannot open program database`.
- Add `C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin` to PATH so **awk** is found, or libpng
  cannot generate `pngprefix.h` (`-DPNG_PREFIX=` in deps/PNG/PNG.cmake) and you
  get a confusing `C1083` on a header that was never written.
- Set `CMAKE_POLICY_VERSION_MINIMUM=3.5` for CMake 4.x.
- **Do not use the CI deps artifact** — the shipped bundle predates `deps/Eigen`
  and cannot satisfy Eigen 5.0.1. Build deps from source.
- Never hard-stop the VM mid-build: doing so left 622 installed files full of
  NUL bytes and surfaced as fake syntax errors inside Boost headers.
- Qhull is deliberately excluded on MSVC (deps/CMakeLists.txt), so 24/25 is
  complete on Windows.
- To run headless, use the app's own hook rather than dropping DLLs beside the
  exe: `src/OrcaSlicer_app_msvc.cpp` loads `<exedir>\mesa\opengl32.dll` when
  system OpenGL < 2.0. Still force `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe`.

The `Build all` Windows CI job fails at `cmake -G "Visual Studio 17 2022"` with
"could not find any instance of Visual Studio". That is a GitHub runner
environment problem, not `build_release_vs.bat` — the same script selects the
same generator on the VM and configures fine against registered Build Tools.

**MSVC rejects `this` in a nested lambda's init-capture.** Found 2026-09-07 at
commit fbe5963b: `CallAfter([self=wxWeakRef<wxWindow>(this),...])` written INSIDE
another lambda compiled on clang but failed on MSVC with 37 errors, because MSVC
bound that `this` to the enclosing closure object, so it tried to build a
`wxWeakRef<wxWindow>` from a lambda pointer
(`Tracked_class_should_inherit_from_wxTrackable`). Name the object first —
`auto* menu = this;` then capture `menu`. Watch for this pattern whenever a
deferred callback is set up from within another lambda; it is invisible on macOS.

=== README ===
# Windows GUI test VM (GCP) — working harness

Drives a wxWidgets + OpenGL desktop app on a GPU-less Windows VM in GCP,
headlessly: launch it, screenshot it, click it, verify the result.

Verified 2026-09-07 with OrcaSlicer 2.4.2 portable.

## The VM

    instance : jusprin-win-test
    project  : elegoo-backend
    zone     : us-central1-a
    machine  : n2-standard-8, Windows Server 2022, 100GB pd-balanced
    display  : virtual display device ENABLED (required, see below)
    login    : ssh as guitest with ~/.ssh/google_compute_engine

The external IP is ephemeral and CHANGES on every stop/start. Re-read it with:

    gcloud compute instances describe jusprin-win-test --zone=us-central1-a \
      --project=elegoo-backend \
      --format="value(networkInterfaces[0].accessConfigs[0].natIP)"

then update winssh.sh / winscp.sh.

## Four things that had to be solved

1. **OpenGL.** The app hard-requires OpenGL 3.2 (src/slic3r/GUI/OpenGLManager.cpp)
   and exits below it. Stock Windows software rendering reports 1.1. Fix: drop
   Mesa's `opengl32.dll` + `libgallium_wgl.dll` (from pal1000/mesa-dist-win) next
   to the .exe. Reports OpenGL 4.2 on plain CPU.

   Mesa then auto-picks its **d3d12** backend, because the GCE virtual display
   exposes "Microsoft Basic Render Driver" as a D3D12 device — and that path
   crashed on the first frame. run-app.cmd forces the CPU rasterizer with
   `GALLIUM_DRIVER=llvmpipe` and `LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1`.

   Do NOT copy the whole Mesa .7z onto the VM: Windows Defender flags the archive
   as Trojan:Win32/Suschil!rfn and deletes it. Extract the two DLLs elsewhere and
   copy just those — Defender does not object to them, so no AV exclusion is
   needed. (The archive's sha256 matches GitHub's published release digest; the
   detection is a heuristic on the bundle, which also contains Vulkan layers,
   D3D12 compilers and media-foundation encoders we don't use.)

2. **A visible desktop.** A GUI app started from an SSH shell lands in a session
   with no desktop and screenshots come back black. autologon.ps1 creates a local
   admin `guitest` and sets Winlogon AutoAdminLogon so console session 1 is always
   live. Something in the GCE image clears those values after the boot that sets
   them, so startup.ps1 re-applies them on EVERY boot.

3. **Session isolation.** Display APIs, EnumWindows and Get-Process MainWindowTitle
   only see the CALLING session's window station. Run them over SSH and they
   silently report nothing — which reads as "the app has no window" when it does.
   Everything that touches the UI goes through `Invoke-InSession` in harness.ps1,
   which registers a scheduled task with `-LogonType Interactive` so it runs in
   session 1, and writes its output to a file to be read back over SSH.

4. **Resolution.** Without a GCE virtual display device the guest falls back to
   Microsoft Basic Display Adapter with no EDID = 640x480, and the app's own
   window is 760x500. Fix (requires the instance to be STOPPED):

       gcloud compute instances stop   jusprin-win-test --zone=us-central1-a --project=elegoo-backend
       gcloud compute instances update jusprin-win-test --zone=us-central1-a --project=elegoo-backend --enable-display-device
       gcloud compute instances start  jusprin-win-test --zone=us-central1-a --project=elegoo-backend

   Then 1920x1080 is available via set-res.ps1.

## Also required by this app

Microsoft Edge WebView2 runtime is NOT present on a clean Windows Server image.
Without it the app puts up a modal "WebView2 Runtime" prompt and startup blocks
forever. Installed here as 152.0.4191.66 via the Evergreen bootstrapper:

    Invoke-WebRequest "https://go.microsoft.com/fwlink/p/?LinkId=2124703" -OutFile setup.exe
    .\setup.exe /silent /install

This matters more for JusPrin than for stock Orca, since JusPrin's UI is
WebView-based.

## Files

    startup.ps1      GCE windows-startup-script-ps1: OpenSSH, port 22 firewall,
                     authorized_keys, calls autologon.ps1. Runs every boot.
    autologon.ps1    Creates guitest + sets AutoAdminLogon. Idempotent.
    harness.ps1      Invoke-InSession / Take-Screenshot. Source this first.
    screenshot.ps1   Screen capture. Must run in-session.
    probe.ps1        Lists session 1's real windows to C:\guitest\windows.txt.
    focus-app.ps1    Closes leftover task consoles, maximizes the app window.
    click.ps1        Clicks the "x,y" in C:\guitest\click.txt.
    set-res.ps1      Sets 1920x1080. Must run in-session.
    install-app.ps1  Downloads the app, places the Mesa DLLs beside the .exe.
    run-app.cmd      Launches the app with llvmpipe forced, detached.
    winssh.sh        ssh wrapper. winscp.sh: scp wrapper.

## Typical cycle

    ./winscp.sh <local.ps1> guitest@<IP>:C:/guitest/
    ./winssh.sh '. C:\guitest\harness.ps1; Invoke-InSession -TaskName "X" ...'
    ./winssh.sh '. C:\guitest\harness.ps1; Take-Screenshot'
    ./winscp.sh guitest@<IP>:C:/guitest/shot.png ./shot.png

There is no current JusPrin Windows binary to test. The Build all workflow's
Windows job fails at `cmake -G "Visual Studio 17 2022"` with "could not find any
instance of Visual Studio"; last green Windows build was 2026-03-04 and its
artifacts have expired. Either fix that job, or install VS Build Tools on this VM
and build from the cached OrcaSlicer_dep_win64 artifact.

# Re-apply auto-logon on EVERY boot. Something in the GCE Windows image clears
# these Winlogon values after the boot that sets them, so a one-shot "only if
# the user doesn't exist" guard is not enough.
$ErrorActionPreference = "Stop"
Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Web
$user = "guitest"
$pw = [System.Web.Security.Membership]::GeneratePassword(24,6)
$sec = ConvertTo-SecureString $pw -AsPlainText -Force

if (-not (Get-LocalUser -Name $user -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) {
    New-LocalUser -Name $user -Password $sec -FullName "GUI Test" -PasswordNeverExpires -AccountNeverExpires | Out-Null
} else {
    Set-LocalUser -Name $user -Password $sec -PasswordNeverExpires $true
}
# -ErrorAction overrides the Stop preference; "already a member" is fine here.
Add-LocalGroupMember -Group "Administrators" -Member $user -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

$wl = "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon"
Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "AutoAdminLogon"    -Value "1"               -Type String
Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "ForceAutoLogon"    -Value "1"               -Type String
Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "DefaultUserName"   -Value $user             -Type String
Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "DefaultPassword"   -Value $pw               -Type String
Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "DefaultDomainName" -Value $env:COMPUTERNAME -Type String
# AutoLogonCount would make this one-shot; make sure it is absent.
Remove-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "AutoLogonCount" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Don't lock or blank the desktop - a locked session screenshots as the lock screen
Set-ItemProperty -Path $wl -Name "ScreenSaverGracePeriod" -Value "0" -Type String -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
$pol = "HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Personalization"
New-Item -Path $pol -Force | Out-Null
Set-ItemProperty -Path $pol -Name "NoLockScreen" -Value 1 -Type DWord
powercfg /change monitor-timeout-ac 0
powercfg /change standby-timeout-ac 0

Write-Host "[AUTOLOGON] applied for $user"

content.text:
I've measured the box rather than guessed. Here's what's actually true and what I'd do about it.

## What I measured

The disk is the confirmed bottleneck; the CPU is not. A sequential write test on the boot disk got **162 MB/s**, which is essentially exactly the theoretical ceiling for a 100 GB balanced persistent disk (Google's formula is 140 MB/s baseline + 0.28 MB/s per GB = 168 MB/s). The disk is small, and on Google Cloud a small balanced disk is also a *slow* disk — throughput and IOPS scale linearly with the size you provision.

| Measurement | Value | Read |
|---|---|---|
| Machine type | n2-standard-16, 16 vCPU, 64 GB RAM | Not the problem |
| CPU platform | Intel Cascade Lake (2019) | Dated, ~2 generations behind |
| CPU load at idle | 9.7% | Nothing is pegging it |
| Free RAM | 53.5 GB of 64 GB | Not the problem |
| Boot disk | pd-balanced, 100 GB | **Bottleneck** |
| Disk write speed | 162 MB/s (cap: 168) | **Saturated at its size cap** |
| Free space on C: | 39.1 GB of 99.9 GB | Tight — `C:\src` alone is 24 GB |
| Windows Defender | Real-time on, **zero exclusions** | Scanning every compiler output |
| Graphics | Microsoft Basic Display Adapter, no GPU | Remote desktop encodes on CPU |
| Network round-trip from your Mac | **57 ms median** | Every click costs 57 ms minimum |

One correction to something I said mid-investigation: I initially read CPU at 97%, but that came from a Windows API that reports a single unreliable instantaneous sample. The real performance counter says 9.7%. The CPU is idle.

## The fork in the road

"Slow" means two unrelated things here, with unrelated fixes, so tell me which one is biting you:

**If the desktop feels laggy** — windows drag late, typing trails your fingers — that is the 57 ms network round-trip plus CPU-based screen encoding. Adding cores or disk will not change it by one millisecond.

**If builds and file operations are slow** — that is the disk, and it's fixable cheaply.

My guess is you mean the first one, because you just used the graphical desktop. But the disk problem is real regardless and you've also asked for more space, so the plan covers both.

## Plan

### Tier 0 — free, no downtime, do regardless

**Add Defender exclusions** for `C:\src`, the build output directories, `C:\tools`, and the compiler binaries. Right now Windows Defender scans every object file the compiler writes, and there are no exclusions at all. I'd expect a meaningful build speedup from this, but I'm labelling that as expectation, not measurement — the honest test is to time one incremental build before and after. The tradeoff is reduced malware scanning on a machine that pulls source from the internet; on a disposable test VM I think that's fine, but it's your call.

**Tune the remote desktop settings** — enable the "Prioritize H.264/AVC 444 graphics mode" policy and adaptive graphics, and drop the desktop to a lower resolution while you work. This is minutes of work and reclaims some of the lag without any infrastructure change.

### Tier 1 — bigger and faster disk, ~10 minutes, no rebuild, no reinstall

Grow the existing boot disk in place. Resizing a Google Cloud persistent disk is an online operation, and extending the Windows partition afterward is also online — nothing gets recreated, nothing gets reinstalled.

Because speed scales with size, this fixes both of your complaints with one action:

| Disk size | Write throughput | IOPS | vs today |
|---|---|---|---|
| 100 GB (today) | 168 MB/s | 3,600 | — |
| 250 GB | 210 MB/s | 4,500 | 1.25x |
| **500 GB** | **280 MB/s** | **6,000** | **1.7x** |
| 1 TB | 420 MB/s | 9,000 | 2.5x |

I'd go to 500 GB: it takes free space from 39 GB to 439 GB and raises the measured ceiling by about 70%.

One caveat I want to flag rather than paper over: every VM also has its own disk performance ceiling based on vCPU count, and I could not find the exact number for a 16-vCPU N2 in Google's docs. So the gain from a very large disk may cap out before the table suggests. At 500 GB I'm confident it won't; at 1 TB it might, and that's worth confirming before paying for it.

### Tier 2 — newer, faster CPU

Your CPU is a 2019 Cascade Lake part. Newer families are available in your zone right now. There are two paths, and they differ a lot in risk:

**Low risk: move to C3.** C3 uses fourth-generation Intel Xeon (Sapphire Rapids) and accepts your existing persistent disk, so this is stop the VM → change the machine type → start. `c3-standard-22` gives you 22 vCPUs and 88 GB. No disk migration, no reinstall, maybe five minutes of downtime.

**Bigger jump, more work: move to C4 or N4.** These use Emerald Rapids or Granite Rapids and are materially faster per core. But I could not confirm from Google's documentation whether they accept a standard persistent disk as a boot disk or require the newer Hyperdisk format — the docs I checked are explicit that the C4D series is Hyperdisk-only but are silent about C4 and N4. **This needs verifying before committing**, and the cheap way is to create one throwaway instance with that machine type and a balanced boot disk and see whether the API rejects it. If they do require Hyperdisk, this becomes a snapshot-and-rebuild job rather than a stop/start — but Hyperdisk has a genuine upside, since it lets you set IOPS and throughput independently of capacity instead of having to buy size to get speed.

### Tier 3 — only if the lag is what's bothering you

Move the VM closer to you. It currently sits in Iowa, 57 ms away. If you're on the US west coast, Oregon or Los Angeles would typically land around 20–30 ms — call that an expectation based on typical routing, not something I measured. Confirm it first by loading `gcping.com` in your browser, which reports live round-trip times to every Google region in a few seconds.

The work is a rebuild, not a resize: snapshot the disk, create a new disk from that snapshot in the target region, create the instance there. Snapshots are global, so this is straightforward, maybe 30 minutes. Everything installed — Claude Code, the desktop app, the toolchain, the source tree — comes across intact.

A hardware video encoder would be the other lag fix, but it needs a GPU, and GPUs don't attach to the N2, C3, or C4 families. That would mean a different machine family and a virtual-workstation license, which I don't think is worth it for this use.

## One cost consideration that should shape the choice

Disk is billed continuously, including while the VM is stopped. CPU is only billed while it runs. Since this VM sits stopped most of the time, a 500 GB disk costs you money every day whether you use it or not, while a faster CPU costs nothing on the days you don't boot it.

Separately, Windows Server licensing on Google Cloud is charged per vCPU. That means jumping from 16 to 32 cores raises your bill by more than the raw compute difference. I'd rather get speed from *faster* cores (Tier 2) than from *more* cores.

I'd suggest confirming the actual figures in Google's pricing calculator before you commit — I don't want to quote you dollar amounts from memory.

## What I'd actually do

Tier 0 today, since it's free and reversible. Then Tier 1 at 500 GB, which is ten minutes and solves the disk complaint outright. Then decide between Tier 2 and Tier 3 based on your answer to the fork above — if the lag is the real irritant, region beats CPU, and it isn't close.

        [System.IO.FileOptions]::WriteThrough)
    for ($i = 0; $i -lt ($mb / 4); $i++) { $fs.Write($buf, 0, $buf.Length) }
    $fs.Flush($true); $fs.Close()
}

$jobs = @()
$sw = [Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
for ($t = 0; $t -lt $Threads; $t++) {

}

$jobs | Remove-Job

content.text:
Both tiers are done, and every claim below is a measurement rather than an estimate. The disk is now 500 GB with 438.5 GB free (was 39.1 GB free), and Windows Defender no longer scans the build tree, which nearly doubled small-file write speed. No downtime and no reboot — the VM stayed up throughout, and the Claude desktop app is still running on it.

## Results

| Measurement | Before | After | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Free space on C: | 39.1 GB | **438.5 GB** | 11x |
| Small-file writes (compile output) | 545 files/s | **988 files/s** | 1.8x |
| Small-file reads | 979 files/s | **2,351 files/s** | 2.4x |
| Disk write throughput | 168 MB/s (ceiling) | **262 MB/s** | 1.6x |

## What I changed

**Defender exclusions.** Added `C:\src`, `C:\tools`, and `C:\guitest` as path exclusions, plus the compiler and build binaries as process exclusions (`cl.exe`, `link.exe`, `lib.exe`, `mspdbsrv.exe`, `rc.exe`, `midl.exe`, `MSBuild.exe`, `ninja.exe`, `cmake.exe`, `ctest.exe`, `git.exe`). Real-time protection remains on everywhere else, so downloads and the rest of the system are still scanned.

I measured this properly: same benchmark, same disk, exclusions the only variable. Writing 2,000 object-file-sized files went from 3.67 s to 2.04 s.

**Disk resized 100 → 500 GB.** Done online at the Google Cloud layer, then the C: partition extended to fill it. C: was the last partition on the disk with no recovery partition in the way, so it extended cleanly.

**Remote desktop codec.** Set `AVC444ModePreferred` to 1, which forces the H.264 codec for full desktop sessions instead of the older bitmap-oriented ones. This takes effect on your *next* connection, so disconnect and reconnect to get it.

## One thing worth knowing, because it nearly fooled me

My first measurement after the resize showed 185 MB/s against a predicted 280 — which reads as "the resize accomplished nothing." That was my benchmark being wrong, not the disk. A single synchronous writer waits for each write to complete before issuing the next, so it measures round-trip latency to Google's storage backend, not how much the disk can actually move. Running eight concurrent writers — which is what a 16-way parallel build does — showed 262 MB/s.

The improvement is real and I can bound it: the old 100 GB disk's hard ceiling was 168 MB/s, and a *single* thread already hit 162 of that, so no amount of concurrency could have exceeded ~168. The new disk sustains 262 MB/s aggregate, above what the old one could reach at any concurrency.

## What this does not fix

The desktop will still feel laggy, because the cause is the 57 ms network round-trip between your Mac and Iowa, and none of today's changes touch that. The H.264 setting will help a little with image quality and bandwidth, but it cannot reduce latency. If the lag is what actually bothers you, the fix is Tier 3 — rebuilding the VM in a west-coast region — and I'd suggest checking `gcping.com` from your browser first to confirm what you'd actually gain.

One cost note: that disk now bills for 500 GB continuously, including while the VM is stopped, at roughly $50/month at typical balanced-disk pricing. Worth confirming in the pricing calculator rather than taking my figure for it.
